lessons.title: Bacterial Cell Structure and the Gram Stain
body: Bacteria are prokaryotes: they have no membrane-bound nucleus, a single circular chromosome in a nucleoid, 70S ribosomes (a 30S and a 50S subunit), and no mitochondria. Those differences from eukaryotic cells are the basis of selective toxicity, because many antibiotics target structures that human cells lack.

The cell envelope is the most clinically important structure. All bacteria have a cytoplasmic membrane. Outside it lies a cell wall of peptidoglycan, a mesh of alternating N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid chains cross-linked by short peptide bridges. The cross-linking step is performed by transpeptidases, also called penicillin-binding proteins, which is why beta-lactams weaken the wall and cause lysis in growing cells.

Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer that also carries teichoic and lipoteichoic acids. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer sandwiched between the inner membrane and an outer membrane. The outer membrane is an asymmetric bilayer whose outer leaflet contains lipopolysaccharide (LPS): lipid A (the endotoxin, which triggers TLR4 signalling and can produce fever and septic shock), a core polysaccharide, and a variable O antigen. Porins in the outer membrane let small hydrophilic molecules through, and the space between the membranes is the periplasm, which holds enzymes such as beta-lactamases.

In the Gram stain, crystal violet and iodine form a complex that is retained by the thick wall of Gram-positive cells after alcohol decolorisation, so they stay purple. Gram-negative cells lose the complex when alcohol dissolves the outer membrane and washes it out of the thin wall, then take up the red safranin counterstain. Organisms that stain poorly are important exceptions: mycobacteria have mycolic acid in the wall and need acid-fast stains; Mycoplasma has no wall; spirochetes are too thin; Chlamydia and Rickettsia are obligate intracellular; Legionella is poorly stained by safranin.

Other structures matter for virulence. A polysaccharide capsule (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis, Klebsiella) resists phagocytosis, and capsular polysaccharide vaccines are made from it. Flagella give motility, and pili or fimbriae mediate adhesion; the sex pilus carries out conjugation. Endospores, formed by Bacillus and Clostridium when nutrients run out, are dormant, dehydrated, dipicolinic acid rich structures that survive boiling and common disinfectants, so killing them requires steam under pressure.

Worked example. A urine isolate stains as pink rods. The pink colour places it among Gram-negatives, whose LPS can provoke endotoxin shock if the organism reaches the blood, and whose outer membrane makes it intrinsically resistant to drugs like vancomycin, which is too large to pass the porins.

lessons.title: Bacterial Growth, Metabolism and Genetics
body: Bacteria divide by binary fission, and in a closed culture growth follows four phases: lag (adaptation), log or exponential (maximal doubling, when cells are most susceptible to cell-wall antibiotics), stationary (nutrient exhaustion balanced against death) and death. Oxygen requirement is a useful classifier. Obligate aerobes (Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Pseudomonas) need oxygen; obligate anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridium) lack superoxide dismutase and catalase and are killed by oxygen; facultative anaerobes (Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus) grow either way; aerotolerant anaerobes (Streptococcus) ferment but tolerate oxygen. Aminoglycosides need an oxygen-dependent uptake system, which is why they are ineffective against anaerobes.

The genome is usually one circular chromosome, but many bacteria carry plasmids: small, circular, self-replicating DNA that often encodes antibiotic resistance, toxins or conjugation machinery. Transposons are mobile elements that move between chromosome and plasmids, and integrons capture gene cassettes, so resistance genes accumulate together.

Bacteria do not reproduce sexually but still exchange DNA by three horizontal routes. Transformation is uptake of naked DNA from the environment by competent cells; Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus and Neisseria are naturally competent, and Griffith's experiment with rough and smooth pneumococci was the classic demonstration. Conjugation transfers DNA through a sex pilus from a donor carrying the F plasmid or a conjugative plasmid; it is the main route of resistance spread among Gram-negatives. Transduction is transfer by bacteriophage. In generalised transduction a phage packages random host DNA by mistake; in specialised transduction a temperate phage excises imprecisely from the chromosome and carries adjacent genes. Lysogenic conversion occurs when a prophage inserted into the chromosome encodes a toxin; the classic examples are diphtheria toxin, botulinum toxin (types C and D), cholera toxin, Shiga toxin and the erythrogenic toxins of Streptococcus pyogenes.
Genetic variation also arises by mutation and, in some pathogens, by phase and antigenic variation, such as the shifting pilin of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and the surface proteins of Borrelia.

Worked example. A patient on therapy for a Klebsiella urinary infection is found to carry an Escherichia coli strain with the same extended-spectrum beta-lactamase gene on a plasmid. The most likely explanation is conjugation between the two Enterobacterales in the gut, not independent mutation in each organism.

Be careful with the vocabulary. Mutation changes one organism's own sequence, whereas horizontal gene transfer brings in DNA, often multiple resistance genes at a time, and can cross species boundaries. That is why resistance can seem to appear suddenly across unrelated strains in one hospital.

lessons.title: Bacterial Virulence Factors and Toxins
body: Virulence is the capacity of an organism to cause disease. Most pathogens follow a sequence: adherence to host surfaces, colonisation, invasion or tissue damage, evasion of host defences, and transmission. Each step has dedicated factors. Adhesins on pili bind receptors on epithelium, and biofilm formation, as in Pseudomonas on catheters and Staphylococcus epidermidis on prosthetic devices, shields organisms from antibiotics. IgA protease, made by Neisseria, Haemophilus and Streptococcus pneumoniae, cleaves mucosal IgA. Protein A of Staphylococcus aureus binds the Fc portion of IgG and blocks opsonisation, and M protein of Streptococcus pyogenes resists phagocytosis. Capsules do the same for encapsulated organisms, and antigenic variation lets the pathogen escape antibody.

Toxins fall into two main groups. Endotoxin is the lipid A component of LPS in Gram-negative outer membranes. It is released with cell death or lysis, acts through TLR4 on macrophages, and produces a cytokine storm: fever, hypotension, activation of the coagulation cascade and, in severe cases, disseminated intravascular coagulation and shock. It is heat stable and poorly converted to a toxoid.

Exotoxins are secreted proteins, mostly heat labile, highly specific and potent, and usually good immunogens whose toxoids make vaccines. Many have A-B structure: the B subunit binds host cell receptors and the A subunit has the enzymatic activity. Key mechanisms to know: Diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A ADP-ribosylate elongation factor 2 and halt protein synthesis. Shiga toxin and the Shiga-like toxin of enterohemorrhagic E. coli cleave an adenine from 28S rRNA of the 60S subunit, blocking protein synthesis. Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gs and locks adenylate cyclase on, so cyclic AMP rises and chloride and water are secreted. Heat-labile toxin of enterotoxigenic E. coli acts the same way, while its heat-stable toxin raises cyclic GMP. Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi, raising cAMP and impairing phagocyte signalling. Anthrax edema factor is an adenylate cyclase. Tetanus and botulinum toxins are zinc-dependent proteases that cleave SNARE proteins: tetanus toxin blocks release of inhibitory glycine and GABA in the spinal cord (spastic paralysis), and botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction (flaccid paralysis). Alpha toxin of Clostridium perfringens is a lecithinase that degrades membranes. Superantigens, such as toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 and streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins, bridge MHC class II and the T cell receptor outside the peptide groove and activate up to a fifth of T cells, causing massive cytokine release.

Worked example. A child with a gray pseudomembrane on the pharynx has toxin that inactivates elongation factor 2. The toxin gene is on a prophage, so only lysogenised Corynebacterium diphtheriae causes this toxic disease.

lessons.title: Host Defense, Normal Flora and Pathogenesis
body: Most of the microbes we carry are harmless or helpful. The skin is dominated by Staphylococcus epidermidis, Cutibacterium acnes and corynebacteria. The oropharynx harbours viridans streptococci, and the nasopharynx holds Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae in carriers, along with Staphylococcus aureus in the anterior nares. The colon is overwhelmingly anaerobic, with Bacteroides and Clostridia outnumbering E. coli by a large margin. The vagina in reproductive-age women is dominated by Lactobacillus, which maintains a low pH. The stomach, lower airway, bladder, blood and deep tissues are normally sterile.

Normal flora protect by colonisation resistance: they compete for nutrients and binding sites, make bacteriocins, and stimulate mucosal immunity. Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt this, which allows overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile in the colon or Candida in the mouth and vagina. Flora also become pathogens when they reach a normally sterile site. Viridans streptococci enter the blood after dental procedures and may seed damaged heart valves, while S. epidermidis infects prosthetic material, and E. coli from the gut ascends the urethra.

Host defence has layers. Barriers include intact skin, mucus and cilia, gastric acid, lysozyme, and urine flow. Innate cells recognise conserved microbial patterns through pattern-recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptors. Complement defects have characteristic infection patterns: C3 deficiency gives severe pyogenic infections, and terminal component (C5 to C9) deficiency predisposes to Neisseria. Splenectomy or functional asplenia removes clearance of encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Haemophilus, meningococcus), so these patients need vaccination. Neutropenia predisposes to Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus, Candida and Aspergillus, while impaired cell-mediated immunity opens the door to intracellular organisms and opportunists such as Pneumocystis, mycobacteria and Listeria.

Koch postulates historically linked a microbe to a disease: the organism is found in every case and not in healthy individuals, is isolated in pure culture, causes disease when introduced into a healthy host, and is re-isolated. They fail for organisms that cannot be cultured, for asymptomatic carriers, and for diseases with multiple causes, so modern molecular criteria supplement them.

Terms to keep straight. Colonisation means presence without disease. Infection means invasion with host response. A pathogen is an organism that regularly causes disease, whereas an opportunist causes disease mainly in a compromised host. Incubation period is the time from exposure to symptoms.

Worked example. A man with a prosthetic knee develops an indolent infection with Staphylococcus epidermidis. This skin commensal is rarely invasive, but its biofilm on foreign material makes it a pathogen when a device is present.

lessons.title: Staphylococci and Streptococci
body: Staphylococci are catalase-positive Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase-positive and ferments mannitol; coagulase-negative species include S. epidermidis (novobiocin-sensitive, prosthetic device infections) and S. saprophyticus (novobiocin-resistant, urinary tract infection in young sexually active women). S. aureus causes skin and soft tissue infection, abscess, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, endocarditis (classically in people who inject drugs, on the tricuspid valve) and pneumonia. Its toxin diseases are food poisoning from preformed enterotoxin (onset within a few hours, vomiting, no fever), toxic shock syndrome from TSST-1 superantigen, and scalded skin syndrome from exfoliative toxin that cleaves desmoglein 1 in the epidermis. Methicillin resistance arises from the mecA gene, which encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with low affinity for beta-lactams; MRSA is therefore resistant to nearly all beta-lactams except specific anti-MRSA cephalosporins, and treatment choices depend on susceptibility testing.

Streptococci are catalase-negative cocci in chains and are classified by hemolysis. Alpha-hemolytic species (partial, green zone) include Streptococcus pneumoniae, optochin-sensitive and bile-soluble, a lancet-shaped diplococcus with a capsule that causes lobar pneumonia, otitis media, sinusitis and meningitis, and the viridans group, optochin-resistant, which causes dental caries and subacute endocarditis on previously damaged valves. Streptococcus mutans produces glucans that anchor plaque. Beta-hemolytic species (complete lysis) are grouped by Lancefield carbohydrate. Group A, Streptococcus pyogenes, is bacitracin-sensitive and PYR-positive. It causes pharyngitis, impetigo, erysipelas, cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis and scarlet fever (erythrogenic toxin, sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue). Immune sequelae follow infection: rheumatic fever (after pharyngitis; molecular mimicry between M protein and cardiac antigens; Jones criteria) and acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (after pharyngitis or skin infection; immune complex deposition, low C3). Antistreptolysin O titres confirm recent pharyngeal infection. Group B, Streptococcus agalactiae, is bacitracin-resistant and hippurate-positive, colonises the vagina, and causes neonatal sepsis and meningitis; intrapartum prophylaxis is guided by screening. Enterococci (group D by antigen) tolerate bile and salt, cause
urinary and biliary infections and endocarditis, and vancomycin-resistant strains are a major hospital problem. Streptococcus bovis (gallolyticus) bacteremia is associated with colon neoplasia.

Worked example. A 9-year-old has sore throat, then three weeks later facial puffiness and cola-coloured urine with low serum C3. This is poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, an immune complex disease, so penicillin therapy of the original infection does not reverse it, but it does reduce spread.
Careful comparison. Rheumatic fever follows only pharyngeal infection and the damage is cross-reactive antibody and T cell response, whereas glomerulonephritis can follow skin infection too.

lessons.title: Gram-Positive Rods and Anaerobes
body: Gram-positive rods divide into spore-formers, non-spore-formers and branching filamentous forms. Bacillus anthracis is an aerobic spore-forming rod with a poly-D-glutamate capsule and a three-part toxin: protective antigen binds host receptors and delivers edema factor (an adenylate cyclase) and lethal factor (a protease that cleaves MAP kinase kinases). Cutaneous anthrax gives a painless black eschar, while inhalational anthrax (woolsorters disease) causes hemorrhagic mediastinitis with a widened mediastinum on chest radiograph. Bacillus cereus causes fried-rice food poisoning: an emetic form from preformed toxin with short incubation, and a diarrheal form from a heat-labile enterotoxin.

Clostridia are anaerobic spore-forming rods. Clostridium tetani, a soil organism, enters through wounds and causes tetanus: trismus, risus sardonicus and opisthotonus through tetanospasmin blocking inhibitory neurotransmitter release. Prevention is by toxoid vaccination and, in high-risk wounds, human tetanus immune globulin. Clostridium botulinum produces botulinum toxin; foodborne botulism comes from preformed toxin in home-canned foods, and infant botulism comes from ingested spores in honey or soil that germinate in the infant gut. The picture is descending symmetric flaccid paralysis with cranial nerve palsies, dilated pupils and no sensory loss. Clostridium perfringens causes gas gangrene (alpha toxin, a lecithinase, with crepitus and a double zone of hemolysis) and a self-limited food poisoning from reheated meat dishes. Clostridioides difficile causes antibiotic-associated colitis through toxins A and B, which glucosylate Rho GTPases and disrupt the cytoskeleton; pseudomembranes are seen at endoscopy, and diagnosis rests on stool toxin or toxin gene testing in a symptomatic patient. Risk factors include clindamycin, cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones, but any antibiotic and hospitalisation increase risk.

Corynebacterium diphtheriae has club-shaped rods in palisades, grows on tellurite or Loeffler medium, and the Elek test detects toxin; the toxin is encoded by a lysogenic phage. Listeria monocytogenes is a tumbling-motile, beta-hemolytic, facultatively intracellular rod; it grows at refrigerator temperature, is acquired from soft cheeses, deli meats and unpasteurised dairy, and causes neonatal sepsis, meningitis in neonates and older or immunocompromised adults, and febrile gastroenteritis. It polymerises host actin (actin rockets) to move cell to cell, and pregnant patients are at risk. Ampicillin is the usual agent because cephalosporins are inactive against it.

Actinomyces israelii is an anaerobic, filamentous, non-acid-fast branching organism that forms sulfur granules and draining sinuses at the jaw after dental trauma. Nocardia asteroides is an aerobic, weakly acid-fast branching organism that causes pulmonary disease and brain abscess in immunocompromised hosts. Distinguish the two by oxygen use and acid-fastness, and note the different treatment: sulfonamides for Nocardia, penicillin for Actinomyces.
Worked example. An infant of 5 months is hypotonic with constipation and a weak cry, after eating honey. The mechanism is blocked acetylcholine release by botulinum toxin.

lessons.title: Neisseria and the Enteric Gram-Negative Rods
body: Neisseria are Gram-negative diplococci that are oxidase-positive. Neisseria meningitidis has a polysaccharide capsule, ferments maltose and glucose, and causes meningitis and meningococcemia, with petechiae and purpura, and in fulminant cases Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome with adrenal hemorrhage and shock. Spread is by respiratory droplets in crowded settings such as dormitories, and complement terminal component deficiency predisposes to recurrent infection. Close contacts receive chemoprophylaxis, and vaccines cover capsular groups A, C, W and Y, and a separate vaccine covers group B. Neisseria gonorrhoeae ferments glucose only, has no capsule, uses pilus antigenic variation to escape immunity, and causes urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, septic arthritis and neonatal conjunctivitis. Because there is no lasting immunity, reinfection is common, and co-testing for Chlamydia is routine. Selective media (Thayer-Martin) support growth.

Enterobacterales are facultatively anaerobic Gram-negative rods that ferment glucose and are oxidase-negative. Lactose fermenters on MacConkey agar (pink) include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella and Enterobacter; non-fermenters (colourless) include Salmonella, Shigella, Proteus and Yersinia. E. coli is the commonest cause of urinary tract infection through uropathogenic strains with P fimbriae. Other pathotypes include enterotoxigenic (travellers diarrhea, heat-labile and heat-stable toxins), enterohemorrhagic O157:H7 (Shiga toxin, bloody diarrhea, hemolytic uremic syndrome, does not ferment sorbitol on sorbitol-MacConkey, and antibiotics may raise HUS risk), enteroinvasive (dysentery like Shigella) and enteropathogenic (infants). E. coli K1 capsule and group B streptococcus cause neonatal meningitis. Klebsiella pneumoniae has a large mucoid capsule, causes pneumonia in alcohol use disorder with currant-jelly sputum, and urinary infection; Klebsiella and Enterobacter often carry ESBL or carbapenemase genes. Proteus is highly motile (swarming), produces urease, raises urine pH, and forms struvite stones.

Salmonella is a motile rod that produces hydrogen sulfide. Nontyphoidal serotypes cause self-limited enterocolitis from poultry, eggs and reptiles and cause osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease. Salmonella Typhi causes enteric fever with a stepwise fever, rose spots, relative bradycardia and bowel perforation; carriage persists in the gallbladder. Shigella is non-motile, makes Shiga toxin (most by Shigella dysenteriae type 1) and invades the colon with a very low infectious dose, causing bloody, mucoid stools. Yersinia enterocolitica causes enterocolitis that can mimic appendicitis. Vibrio and Campylobacter are curved forms handled in the next lesson.

Worked example. A 4-year-old has bloody diarrhea after a hamburger and then oliguria, anemia with schistocytes and thrombocytopenia. This is hemolytic uremic syndrome from Shiga toxin of E. coli O157:H7, which damages endothelium, so antibiotics and antimotility agents are avoided.

lessons.title: Other Gram-Negative Pathogens
body: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an aerobic, oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting rod that makes blue-green pigment (pyocyanin) and a grape-like odour. It colonises moist environments, forms biofilms, and causes burn wound and hospital-acquired infection, ventilator pneumonia, otitis externa (swimmers ear), folliculitis from hot tubs, and chronic lung infection in cystic fibrosis, where mucoid alginate strains predominate. Ecthyma gangrenosum is a necrotic skin lesion in bacteremia. Exotoxin A blocks elongation factor 2. It is intrinsically resistant to many agents, and treatment needs an antipseudomonal drug chosen by susceptibility results.

Vibrio cholerae is a comma-shaped, oxidase-positive rod that grows in alkaline media (TCBS) and is acquired from contaminated water; its toxin causes massive rice-water diarrhea, and rehydration is the cornerstone of therapy. Vibrio vulnificus causes wound infection and septicemia after raw oyster consumption or seawater exposure, with severe risk in liver disease or iron overload. Campylobacter jejuni is a curved microaerophilic rod growing at 42 C that causes bloody diarrhea from undercooked poultry and is a recognised trigger of Guillain-Barre syndrome. Helicobacter pylori is a curved, urease-positive, oxidase-positive rod that colonises gastric antrum mucosa; the urease releases ammonia that buffers acid. It causes chronic gastritis, duodenal and gastric ulcer, gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma. Diagnostic tests include urea breath test, stool antigen and biopsy urease testing; eradication uses combination regimens that include a proton pump inhibitor, and local resistance patterns shape the choice.

Haemophilus influenzae is a small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacillus needing factor X (hemin) and factor V (NAD) on chocolate agar. Encapsulated type b caused epiglottitis, meningitis and sepsis in unvaccinated children before the conjugate vaccine; unencapsulated nontypable strains cause otitis media, sinusitis and exacerbations of chronic obstructive lung disease. Bordetella pertussis is a small aerobic coccobacillus causing whooping cough: catarrhal, paroxysmal (inspiratory whoop, post-tussive vomiting) and convalescent stages, with marked lymphocytosis from pertussis toxin; vaccination in pregnancy protects newborns. Legionella pneumophila lives in warm water systems, is acquired by inhaling aerosols rather than person to person, stains poorly, grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar with iron and cysteine, and causes pneumonia with fever, confusion, diarrhea and hyponatremia. Urinary antigen testing is the standard rapid diagnosis for serogroup 1.

Other points to remember: Moraxella catarrhalis is an oxidase-positive diplococcus in otitis and COPD exacerbations. Acinetobacter is a nosocomial, often multidrug-resistant coccobacillus. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is intrinsically resistant to carbapenems.

Worked example. A 66-year-old man returns from a cruise with fever, confusion, diarrhea, patchy pneumonia and a serum sodium of 128 mmol/L. Legionella pneumonia is likely, so the urinary antigen is ordered and a macrolide or fluoroquinolone, which penetrate cells, is chosen rather than a beta-lactam.

lessons.title: Mycobacteria
body: Mycobacteria are aerobic, non-motile rods whose wall is rich in mycolic acids, long-chain fatty acids that make the organism acid-fast (retaining carbol fuchsin after acid-alcohol, as in the Ziehl-Neelsen stain), hydrophobic and resistant to many disinfectants. They grow slowly; M. tuberculosis divides about once a day, so cultures take weeks, and Lowenstein-Jensen or liquid media are used. Cord factor (trehalose dimycolate) is a virulence factor, and sulfatides inhibit phagosome-lysosome fusion.

Tuberculosis is spread by aerosolised droplet nuclei. In the lung the organism is taken up by alveolar macrophages and survives inside them. Infection leads to a primary (Ghon) focus, usually in the lower or mid lung, with hilar lymph node involvement, together called the Ghon complex. About 2 to 3 weeks later cell-mediated immunity develops: macrophages activated by interferon gamma from Th1 cells wall off the bacilli in granulomas with central caseous necrosis, Langhans giant cells and epithelioid cells. In most people this is latent infection. Reactivation (secondary TB) occurs when immunity wanes, as with HIV, steroid or TNF inhibitor therapy, and typically affects the apices, where oxygen tension is high, producing cavitation. Spread through blood gives miliary tuberculosis, and extrapulmonary sites include spine (Pott disease), meninges, kidney (sterile pyuria), adrenal glands and lymph nodes (scrofula). Symptoms are chronic cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats and weight loss.

Diagnosis. The tuberculin skin test measures delayed type hypersensitivity, read at 48 to 72 hours as induration, with a size threshold that depends on risk group; false positives follow BCG vaccination and nontuberculous exposure, and false negatives follow immunosuppression. Interferon gamma release assays use specific antigens absent from BCG and most environmental mycobacteria. Active disease is confirmed by smear, culture and nucleic acid amplification, and by chest imaging. Treatment of active disease uses multiple drugs for months to prevent resistance, and standard first-line agents include rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol; adverse effects include hepatotoxicity (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide), peripheral neuropathy (isoniazid, prevented with pyridoxine), optic neuritis (ethambutol), and orange body fluids and cytochrome P450 induction (rifampin). Multidrug resistance means resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampin and needs specialist regimens. Latent infection may be treated to prevent reactivation. BCG is a live attenuated vaccine used in many countries.

Nontuberculous mycobacteria include Mycobacterium avium complex (disseminated infection in advanced HIV with low CD4 counts, and bronchiectasis in others), Mycobacterium kansasii (cavitary disease resembling tuberculosis), Mycobacterium marinum (swimming pool granuloma, fish tank, cool skin) and rapid growers like M. abscessus. M. leprae grows in cool tissues and in armadillos, cannot be cultured on artificial media, and causes leprosy: tuberculoid disease (strong Th1 response, few bacilli, localised anesthetic skin lesions) and lepromatous disease (weak cell-mediated immunity, many bacilli, diffuse lesions and leonine facies). Diagnosis uses skin biopsy and acid-fast stain, and multidrug treatment is standard.

Worked example. A 45-year-old man with HIV, CD4 count 40 cells per microliter, has fever, weight loss and anemia. Blood cultures grow acid-fast organisms. The likely organism is Mycobacterium avium complex, not M. tuberculosis, since the CD4 count is very low and the disease is disseminated.

lessons.title: Spirochetes
body: Spirochetes are thin, helical, motile bacteria with periplasmic flagella (axial filaments), so they stain poorly with Gram stain and are seen by darkfield microscopy, silver stain, or fluorescent antibody. The medically important genera are Treponema, Borrelia and Leptospira.

Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum causes syphilis. It cannot be cultured in vitro and is transmitted sexually or from mother to fetus. Primary syphilis begins after about 3 weeks as a painless firm ulcer (chancre) with regional lymphadenopathy. Secondary syphilis occurs weeks later with a diffuse maculopapular rash that includes palms and soles, mucous patches, condylomata lata (highly infectious) and fever; it is a systemic bacteremia. Then comes a latent period of years. Tertiary syphilis includes gummas (granulomatous lesions), cardiovascular syphilis (aortitis of the ascending aorta with aneurysm) and neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis with loss of position sense and Argyll Robertson pupils, general paresis). Congenital syphilis can cause stillbirth, Hutchinson teeth, saddle nose and deafness. Diagnosis uses a nontreponemal test (RPR or VDRL, detecting antibodies to cardiolipin, titre rising and falling with activity, subject to biologic false positives in pregnancy, lupus and some infections) followed by a treponemal test (FTA-ABS, TP-PA, or treponemal EIA), which remains positive for life; many labs run the sequence in reverse. Penicillin remains the treatment of choice. The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is fever and worsening symptoms hours after the first dose, caused by release of bacterial products from dying spirochetes. Nonvenereal treponematoses include yaws, pinta and bejel.

Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease, transmitted by Ixodes ticks (deer tick) that must usually feed for more than a day. The pattern is early localised disease with erythema migrans (expanding annular rash, often with central clearing), early disseminated disease with multiple lesions, facial nerve palsy (possibly bilateral), meningitis, and heart block, and late disease with migratory large-joint arthritis, especially the knee. Reservoirs include white-footed mice and deer. Serology uses a two-tier approach, and clinical judgement guides early diagnosis because antibodies lag. Treatment is oral doxycycline in most adults and children above eight years, with other options for pregnancy. Borrelia recurrentis and others cause relapsing fever through antigenic variation of surface proteins, with recurrent febrile episodes.

Leptospira interrogans enters through broken skin or mucosa from water contaminated by urine of rats, dogs and livestock. Mild disease is a biphasic fever with conjunctival suffusion, and severe disease (Weil disease) combines jaundice, renal failure and hemorrhage, with pulmonary hemorrhage in some outbreaks. Occupational and recreational freshwater exposure is typical.

Worked example. A 31-year-old man has a painless genital ulcer. Darkfield microscopy shows motile spirals, and the RPR is positive at a high titre. After penicillin, he has chills and fever within hours. This reaction does not represent allergy; it reflects endotoxin-like release as the organisms die.

lessons.title: Rickettsiae, Chlamydiae, Mycoplasma and Related Intracellular Bacteria
body: Several bacteria are poorly seen on Gram stain because they live inside cells or lack a conventional wall. Rickettsiae are small Gram-negative-like obligate intracellular bacteria that infect endothelial cells of small vessels, causing vasculitis, rash and edema. They are arthropod-borne. Rickettsia rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever from Dermacentor ticks, and despite the name is most common in the southeastern and south-central United States; fever, headache and a rash that begins on wrists and ankles and spreads centrally to include palms and soles. Treatment with doxycycline should not wait for confirmation. Rickettsia prowazekii (louse-borne epidemic typhus) and Rickettsia typhi (flea-borne murine typhus) cause typhus. Orientia tsutsugamushi causes scrub typhus with an eschar from chigger bites. The Weil-Felix test used proteus antigens and is historical. Ehrlichia and Anaplasma infect leukocytes (monocytes and granulocytes respectively) and form intracellular clusters called morulae, causing fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised liver enzymes. Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever, acquired by inhalation of aerosols from livestock birthing products and not by a vector, and results in atypical pneumonia, hepatitis and culture-negative endocarditis. It forms a resistant spore-like form. Bartonella henselae causes cat-scratch disease (regional lymphadenopathy) and, in advanced HIV, bacillary angiomatosis, a vascular proliferation.

Chlamydiae have a biphasic life cycle. The elementary body is the infectious, metabolically inactive extracellular form, which enters a cell and reorganises into the reticulate body, the replicating form, inside an inclusion; reticulate bodies then condense into new elementary bodies. They cannot make their own ATP efficiently and are energy parasites. Chlamydia trachomatis serovars A to C cause trachoma (follicular conjunctivitis and scarring, leading to blindness), D to K cause urogenital infection (cervicitis, urethritis, PID, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia), and L1 to L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum with painful inguinal buboes. Diagnosis is by nucleic acid amplification, and doxycycline or azithromycin are used. Chlamydophila (Chlamydia) pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia, and Chlamydia psittaci causes psittacosis from birds.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae has no cell wall, so it stains poorly, is insensitive to beta-lactams, and has sterols in its membrane. It causes walking pneumonia in young adults, with a dry cough, a radiograph worse than the symptoms, and sometimes cold agglutinins (IgM against the I antigen on red cells, with hemolytic anemia), and Stevens-Johnson syndrome or erythema multiforme. Macrolides, doxycycline or respiratory fluoroquinolones are used. Ureaplasma and Mycoplasma genitalium are associated with urethritis.

Worked example. A 20-year-old has a slowly worsening dry cough for two weeks, low-grade fever and patchy infiltrates, with a Gram stain showing few organisms. The cold agglutinin titre is raised. Mycoplasma is likely, so a beta-lactam would fail because the organism has no peptidoglycan target.

lessons.title: Zoonotic and Vector-Borne Bacterial Infections
body: Zoonoses are infections that pass from animals to humans, and the history of exposure often supplies the diagnosis. A useful approach is to link the animal or arthropod to the organism and then to the syndrome.

Brucella species are small Gram-negative coccobacilli that are intracellular and are acquired from unpasteurised dairy or from contact with infected livestock, goats, sheep, cattle or pigs, and are an occupational hazard for farmers, slaughterhouse workers and veterinarians. The disease is undulant fever, with relapsing fever, sweats, arthralgia, sacroiliitis, hepatosplenomegaly and sometimes orchitis or endocarditis. Culture needs prolonged incubation, so laboratories are alerted when brucellosis is suspected. Treatment is combination therapy to prevent relapse.

Francisella tularensis, a tiny Gram-negative coccobacillus, causes tularemia, acquired from rabbits and hares, from tick and deer fly bites, and by inhalation. Ulceroglandular tularemia is the commonest form: a skin ulcer with regional lymphadenopathy. Very low infectious doses make it a laboratory hazard and a recognised biothreat. Yersinia pestis causes plague, from rodent flea bites; in the United States, small mammals in the Southwest are the reservoir. Bubonic plague has painful inflamed lymph nodes (buboes), septicemic plague causes sepsis and gangrene, and pneumonic plague spreads person to person by droplets and is rapidly fatal without treatment. The organism shows bipolar staining (safety pin appearance). Pasteurella multocida causes rapidly developing cellulitis within a day after a cat or dog bite, so bite wounds are covered with an antibiotic that includes it. Capnocytophaga canimorsus can cause overwhelming sepsis after dog bites in asplenic patients and those with alcohol use disorder. Bartonella henselae is spread by cat scratches and fleas. Coxiella burnetii and Chlamydia psittaci come from livestock and birds respectively, as covered earlier. Streptobacillus moniliformis causes rat-bite fever.

Vector-borne bacteria in the Ixodes and Amblyomma ticks include Borrelia burgdorferi, Anaplasma phagocytophilum (Ixodes) and Ehrlichia chaffeensis (Amblyomma, the lone star tick). Co-infection of Borrelia with Anaplasma or the protozoan Babesia can occur because they share the Ixodes vector. Clues differentiate them: cytopenias with morulae favour Anaplasma or Ehrlichia, a spreading annular rash favours Lyme, and a centripetal petechial rash favours Rocky Mountain spotted fever.

Public health points. Pathogens such as Bacillus anthracis, Yersinia pestis, Francisella tularensis and Brucella are agents of concern for bioterrorism, and a suspected case triggers notification of health authorities and communication with the laboratory. Prevention rests on animal vaccination, pasteurisation, vector control, and personal protection.

Worked example. A 38-year-old rancher has three weeks of evening fevers and sweats, low back pain, and joint pain. He drinks raw goat milk. Blood cultures held for extended incubation grow tiny Gram-negative coccobacilli. This is brucellosis, and treatment uses two drugs over a long course because monotherapy relapses.

lessons.title: Viral Structure, Replication and DNA Viruses
body: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites made of a nucleic acid genome (DNA or RNA, single or double stranded) inside a protein capsid, with an outer lipid envelope in some. Enveloped viruses are fragile, spread by close contact, secretions and droplets, and are inactivated by drying, detergents and alcohol; naked viruses (adenovirus, norovirus, picornaviruses) survive harsh conditions, resist alcohol hand rubs and spread by the fecal-oral route and surfaces. The replication cycle runs through attachment to a receptor, entry, uncoating, genome replication and expression, assembly and release. Release of enveloped viruses is by budding, and naked viruses are usually released by lysis.

Genome rules help prediction. Most DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus and use host polymerases; poxviruses are the exception and replicate in the cytoplasm with their own enzymes, and hepadnaviruses use reverse transcriptase. Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm using viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, and influenza and retroviruses are exceptions with nuclear steps. Positive-sense RNA genomes act directly as mRNA and are infectious as naked RNA; negative-sense genomes must carry their polymerase in the virion. Segmented genomes (influenza, rotavirus) allow reassortment: swapping segments between strains that coinfect one cell, giving antigenic shift. Point mutations produce antigenic drift. Complementation, phenotypic mixing and pseudotyping describe interactions between coinfecting strains.

Adenoviruses are naked double-stranded DNA viruses that cause pharyngitis, acute conjunctivitis, hemorrhagic cystitis, pneumonia in military recruits and epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, and are a cause of childhood diarrhea. Papillomaviruses are small DNA viruses; types 6 and 11 cause genital warts, while 16, 18 and other high-risk types cause cervical, anal and oropharyngeal cancer. E6 binds and degrades p53 and E7 inactivates Rb, so cell cycle control is lost. Vaccines made from virus-like particles of the L1 capsid protein prevent infection, and Papanicolaou smear and HPV testing screen for cervical disease; koilocytes (perinuclear halo with atypical nuclei) are the cytologic hallmark. Polyomaviruses include JC virus (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in severely immunosuppressed people, with demyelination from oligodendrocyte infection) and BK virus (hemorrhagic cystitis and nephropathy in transplant recipients). Parvovirus B19 is a small single-stranded DNA virus that infects erythroid progenitors using the P antigen: erythema infectiosum (fifth disease, slapped-cheek rash) in children, arthropathy in adults, aplastic crisis in people with chronic hemolysis such as sickle cell disease, and hydrops fetalis in pregnancy. Poxviruses are the largest viruses; smallpox (variola) was eradicated, and molluscum contagiosum causes pearly umbilicated papules. Mpox is a zoonotic orthopoxvirus infection with vesiculopustular lesions and lymphadenopathy.

Worked example. A 7-year-old has bright red cheeks followed by a lacy trunk rash with little fever. This is parvovirus B19, and the main danger is in people with high red cell turnover or in pregnancy, because the virus targets erythroid precursors.

lessons.title: Herpesviruses
body: Herpesviruses are enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses that replicate in the nucleus and establish lifelong latency, with reactivation when immunity falls. Eight infect humans. Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) classically causes orolabial lesions, keratitis and encephalitis, and type 2 (HSV-2) causes most recurrent genital herpes and neonatal disease, but each can cause either. Latency is in sensory ganglia: trigeminal for HSV-1, sacral for HSV-2. A Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry A inclusions, though PCR is the preferred test. HSV encephalitis typically affects the temporal lobes, causing fever, personality change and seizures, and CSF PCR confirms it; empirical acyclovir is started immediately. Neonatal herpes is acquired at delivery from a mother with active genital lesions or a primary infection, and may be skin, eye and mouth disease, encephalitis or disseminated infection.

Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) causes chickenpox (vesicles in crops at different stages) on primary infection, and shingles when latent virus in dorsal root ganglia reactivates along a dermatome. Postherpetic neuralgia and zoster ophthalmicus are complications, and congenital varicella can follow maternal infection in early pregnancy. Live varicella vaccine prevents chickenpox, and a recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended for older adults.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a leading congenital infection with hearing loss, microcephaly and periventricular calcifications. In transplant recipients it causes pneumonitis, colitis and retinitis, and in AIDS patients it causes retinitis (fluffy white lesions with hemorrhage). Biopsy shows owl-eye intranuclear inclusions. In immunocompetent adults it can cause a mononucleosis-like illness that is heterophile-negative. Treatment is ganciclovir or related drugs. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects B cells through CD21 and causes infectious mononucleosis: fever, pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly (with splenic rupture risk, so contact sports are avoided) and atypical lymphocytes, which are reactive CD8 T cells; the heterophile (monospot) test is positive but can be falsely negative in young children. EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma and posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder, and oral hairy leukoplakia in HIV. HHV-6 causes roseola (high fever then rash as the fever resolves) and HHV-7 is similar. HHV-8 (KSHV) causes Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma.

Antiviral logic. Acyclovir is a guanosine analogue that requires phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase to become active, so it is selective for infected cells, and it then terminates the DNA chain when incorporated by viral DNA polymerase. Resistance arises by loss of thymidine kinase, in which case foscarnet, a pyrophosphate analogue that does not need activation, is used. Ganciclovir needs the CMV UL97 kinase and is limited by bone marrow suppression. Cidofovir acts without viral kinase and is nephrotoxic. Valacyclovir is a prodrug of acyclovir with better oral bioavailability.

Worked example. A 24-year-old has fever, sore throat, large tonsils with exudate, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes. Amoxicillin was given earlier and a rash appeared. This is classic for infectious mononucleosis, and the rash on aminopenicillin is a recognised association, not true penicillin allergy.

lessons.title: RNA Viruses: Respiratory, Enteric, Arboviral and Emerging
body: Influenza viruses are enveloped, segmented, negative-sense RNA orthomyxoviruses with hemagglutinin (HA, for attachment) and neuraminidase (NA, for release). Types A and B cause seasonal epidemics; type A also infects animals and undergoes antigenic shift by reassortment, which can produce pandemic strains, while antigenic drift explains the need for yearly vaccine updates. Complications include primary viral pneumonia and secondary bacterial pneumonia, notably Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir are most beneficial when started early, and the polymerase endonuclease inhibitor baloxavir is another class. Guillain-Barre syndrome and Reye syndrome (with aspirin in children) are other associations.

Paramyxoviruses are enveloped, negative-sense RNA viruses. Measles is highly contagious and presents with the three Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa, then a maculopapular rash from head to toe; complications are pneumonia, encephalitis and rare subacute sclerosing panencephalitis; vitamin A is given in severe cases. Mumps causes parotitis, orchitis and aseptic meningitis. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes bronchiolitis in infants, forming syncytia; prevention in infants includes maternal vaccination and monoclonal antibody products. Parainfluenza causes croup (steeple sign on neck radiograph). Human metapneumovirus is similar to RSV. Coronaviruses are enveloped, positive-sense RNA viruses with spike proteins that bind receptors; SARS-CoV-2 uses ACE2, and other human coronaviruses are a common cause of colds.

Picornaviruses are naked, positive-sense RNA viruses. Poliovirus replicates in the gut and, in a small minority of infections, destroys anterior horn motor neurons causing asymmetric flaccid paralysis; inactivated and oral vaccines differ in mucosal immunity and the rare vaccine-derived disease. Coxsackieviruses cause hand-foot-and-mouth disease, herpangina, myocarditis (group B) and aseptic meningitis; rhinoviruses cause colds, with acid lability keeping them out of the gut; hepatitis A is also a picornavirus. Enteric viruses: rotavirus, a segmented double-stranded RNA reovirus, is the leading cause of severe childhood diarrhea, with vaccination reducing the burden, and norovirus (a calicivirus) causes outbreaks of vomiting on cruise ships and in institutions.

Arboviruses. Flaviviruses (positive-sense RNA, mosquito or tick transmitted) include yellow fever (jaundice, hemorrhage, with a live attenuated vaccine), dengue (fever, severe myalgia, thrombocytopenia, with risk of plasma leakage and shock, especially on second infection with a different serotype), Zika (congenital microcephaly), West Nile virus (neuroinvasive disease in a minority) and Japanese encephalitis. Hepatitis C is also a flavivirus-family virus (hepacivirus). Togaviruses include rubella (mild rash and posterior auricular nodes, with congenital rubella causing cataracts, deafness and heart defects) and alphaviruses such as chikungunya (severe arthralgia).

Other emerging and zoonotic RNA viruses. Rabies, a bullet-shaped rhabdovirus, spreads from a bite of an infected mammal (bats in many regions), travels up peripheral nerves to the CNS, and causes hydrophobia, agitation and death; Negri bodies are cytoplasmic inclusions. Postexposure prophylaxis consists of wound care, rabies immune globulin and vaccine and works because incubation is long. Filoviruses (Ebola, Marburg) cause hemorrhagic fever with high mortality, spread by contact with body fluids, and vaccines and monoclonal therapy exist for Ebola virus. Hantaviruses spread from rodent excreta and cause pulmonary syndrome. Arenaviruses such as Lassa cause hemorrhagic fever. Prions are not viruses but proteinaceous infectious particles causing spongiform encephalopathies.

Worked example. A 9-month-old in winter has fever, nasal flaring, wheeze and crackles, and nasopharyngeal testing shows a virus that fuses cells into syncytia. This is RSV bronchiolitis, treated with supportive care.

lessons.title: HIV and the Hepatitis Viruses
body: HIV is an enveloped retrovirus with two copies of positive-sense RNA, and reverse transcriptase makes DNA that integrates into the host genome through integrase. The envelope has gp120 (attachment to CD4 and a coreceptor, CCR5 early and CXCR4 later) and gp41 (fusion). The gag gene encodes the capsid protein p24 and other structural proteins, pol encodes reverse transcriptase, protease and integrase, and env encodes the glycoproteins. High error rates and recombination give tremendous diversity. Primary infection often causes a mononucleosis-like illness, followed by clinical latency of years with persistent viral replication in lymphoid tissue; CD4 T cell counts decline, and AIDS is defined by a CD4 count below 200 cells per microliter or an AIDS-defining illness.

Diagnosis uses fourth-generation antigen and antibody assays, which detect p24 antigen and shorten the window period, followed by confirmation with a differentiation immunoassay and nucleic acid testing. In infants born to infected mothers, maternal IgG persists, so nucleic acid testing is used. Viral load tracks treatment response. Antiretroviral therapy combines drugs from classes that block entry, reverse transcription (nucleoside and non-nucleoside inhibitors), integration (integrase inhibitors) or maturation (protease inhibitors); combination therapy prevents resistance, and sustained suppression prevents sexual transmission. Opportunistic infection prophylaxis is guided by CD4 thresholds: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is below 200 (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), toxoplasmosis below about 100, and Mycobacterium avium complex below about 50 in older practice. Other opportunists include cryptococcal meningitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis (ring-enhancing lesions), CMV retinitis, esophageal candidiasis, JC virus PML, and Kaposi sarcoma.

Hepatitis viruses cause liver inflammation with raised transaminases. Hepatitis A (picornavirus, fecal-oral) and hepatitis E (fecal-oral, dangerous in pregnancy) cause acute, self-limited disease without chronic carriage; hepatitis A is confirmed by IgM, and a vaccine exists. Hepatitis B is a partially double-stranded DNA hepadnavirus with a reverse transcriptase, spread by blood, sexual contact and perinatally. Serology: HBsAg appears first and indicates infection; anti-HBs indicates immunity from vaccination or recovery; anti-HBc IgM marks acute infection and may be the only positive marker during the window period; HBeAg indicates high replication and infectivity. Persistence of HBsAg beyond six months defines chronic infection, with cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma risk; infection at birth leads to chronic carriage in most cases, so newborns of infected mothers receive vaccine and immune globulin. Hepatitis D is a defective RNA virus requiring HBsAg and causes coinfection or superinfection with worse disease. Hepatitis C is a positive-sense RNA virus spread mainly by blood exposure, often asymptomatic acutely, with high rates of chronic infection, cirrhosis and carcinoma, and cryoglobulinemia; it varies antigenically so there is no vaccine, and direct-acting antivirals now cure most patients. Screening is recommended for adults by current US guidelines.

Worked example. A patient has HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative and anti-HBc IgM positive. This is the window period of acute hepatitis B, when the surface antigen has cleared before the surface antibody appears, so the core IgM is the only marker.

lessons.title: Medical Mycology
body: Fungi are eukaryotes with chitin in the wall and ergosterol in the membrane, which is why antifungal drugs target ergosterol or the wall glucan. Yeasts are unicellular and divide by budding, molds grow as branching hyphae, and dimorphic fungi are molds at room temperature and yeasts (or spherules) at body temperature, a useful rule: cold is mold, hot is yeast.

Superficial and cutaneous infections. Dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) digest keratin and cause tinea of the scalp, body, groin, feet and nails; diagnosis uses potassium hydroxide preparation showing hyphae. Malassezia furfur causes tinea versicolor, with hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches and a spaghetti-and-meatballs appearance on KOH. Sporothrix schenckii, a dimorphic fungus from roses and soil, causes ascending lymphocutaneous nodules after a thorn prick. Candida albicans is part of the normal flora and forms germ tubes and pseudohyphae; thrush, vulvovaginitis, diaper dermatitis, esophagitis (in AIDS), and candidemia with line infections or after abdominal surgery occur when flora or barriers are disrupted. Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis suggests a T cell defect.

Systemic dimorphic fungi (endemic mycoses) are inhaled and cause pulmonary disease resembling tuberculosis or pneumonia, with dissemination in the immunocompromised. Histoplasma capsulatum (Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, bird and bat droppings) is a small yeast within macrophages; disseminated disease causes hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia. Blastomyces dermatitidis (Great Lakes and Ohio and Mississippi valleys) has broad-based budding yeast and causes pulmonary and skin and bone disease. Coccidioides immitis and posadasii (southwestern United States) form spherules with endospores; desert rheumatism with erythema nodosum and risk of meningitis are features. Paracoccidioides has a pilot-wheel appearance in Latin America. Opportunists: Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast (mucicarmine stain, India ink) from pigeon droppings that causes meningitis in advanced HIV, diagnosed with antigen testing, with high intracranial pressure. Aspergillus fumigatus has septate hyphae with acute-angle branching and causes allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in asthma and cystic fibrosis, aspergilloma in old cavities, and invasive pulmonary disease in neutropenia; aflatoxin from Aspergillus flavus is a hepatocarcinogen. Mucorales (Mucor, Rhizopus) have broad nonseptate hyphae with right-angle branching and cause rhinocerebral mucormycosis in ketoacidosis, with a black

eschar, needing surgical debridement. Pneumocystis jirovecii causes pneumonia in advanced HIV and immunosuppression, with diffuse interstitial infiltrates, high LDH and beta-D-glucan, and silver stain showing cysts; TMP-SMX is used for treatment and prophylaxis.

Antifungals. Amphotericin B binds ergosterol to form membrane pores and is nephrotoxic, with infusion reactions; liposomal formulations lessen toxicity. Azoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole) inhibit fungal cytochrome P450 14-alpha-demethylase, blocking ergosterol synthesis, and cause many drug interactions and hepatotoxicity. Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin) inhibit beta-glucan synthase. Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase and treats dermatophyte nail infection. Flucytosine is converted to 5-fluorouracil in fungi. Griseofulvin disrupts microtubules in dermatophytes.

Worked example. A 33-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes and ketoacidosis has facial pain, black necrotic tissue on the palate and cranial nerve deficits. Biopsy shows broad ribbon-like nonseptate hyphae. This is mucormycosis, so urgent debridement and amphotericin are required, because azoles of the voriconazole type lack activity.

lessons.title: Protozoa
body: Protozoa are single-celled eukaryotes. A practical way to learn them is by body site and vector.

Intestinal protozoa. Giardia lamblia is acquired as cysts from water (campers, daycare); trophozoites with a pear shape and two nuclei attach to the duodenum and cause foul, fatty diarrhea with bloating but no blood, and are diagnosed by stool antigen or cysts and trophozoites in stool. Entamoeba histolytica causes bloody dysentery with flask-shaped colon ulcers and liver abscess ("anchovy paste" pus), from cysts in contaminated water; trophozoites may contain ingested red cells. Both respond to metronidazole, with a luminal agent added for amebiasis. Cryptosporidium (acid-fast oocysts) causes watery diarrhea, chronic and severe in AIDS, and is resistant to chlorine. Cyclospora causes watery diarrhea from fresh produce.

Blood and tissue protozoa. Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito. Sporozoites infect hepatocytes, then merozoites invade red cells, mature through ring, trophozoite and schizont stages, and rupture cells, causing cyclic fever and hemolysis; liver stages (hypnozoites) persist in P. vivax and P. ovale, causing relapse unless primaquine or tafenoquine is used (testing for G6PD deficiency first because of hemolysis risk). P. falciparum is the most dangerous: it infects red cells of all ages, causes high parasitemia, and expresses PfEMP1 that sticks infected cells to endothelium, causing cerebral malaria, severe anemia, renal failure, and hypoglycemia; banana-shaped gametocytes are seen. P. vivax and P. ovale prefer young red cells, and vivax needs the Duffy antigen, so many West Africans are resistant. P. malariae causes quartan fever and nephrotic syndrome. Diagnosis uses thick and thin blood smears and rapid antigen tests. Sickle cell trait and G6PD deficiency confer some protection. Prophylaxis and treatment depend on local drug resistance patterns and on species, with artemisinin combination therapy as a major class. Babesia microti infects red cells (Maltese cross on smear), is transmitted by Ixodes ticks, and causes hemolysis, particularly in asplenic patients.

Trypanosoma brucei gambiense and rhodesiense cause African sleeping sickness through tsetse flies, with antigenic variation of surface glycoproteins. Trypanosoma cruzi is spread by reduviid ("kissing") bugs and causes Chagas disease with acute Romana sign, and chronic cardiomyopathy, megaesophagus and megacolon. Leishmania is spread by sandflies: cutaneous disease, mucocutaneous disease and visceral kala-azar with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia, amastigotes seen in macrophages. Toxoplasma gondii is acquired from cat feces or undercooked meat; infection is mostly asymptomatic or mononucleosis-like, but congenital toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications) and reactivation in AIDS (ring-enhancing brain lesions) are key. Free-living amoebae: Naegleria fowleri enters through the nose in warm freshwater and causes rapidly fatal meningoencephalitis, and Acanthamoeba causes keratitis in contact lens users. Trichomonas vaginalis is a sexually transmitted, motile flagellate causing frothy discharge and a strawberry cervix, treated with metronidazole.

Worked example. A traveller returns from West Africa with fever, headache and confusion. A thin smear shows ring forms with multiple rings in single red cells and banana-shaped gametocytes. This is falciparum malaria, a medical emergency.

lessons.title: Helminths
body: Helminths are multicellular worms. Three groups: nematodes (roundworms), cestodes (tapeworms, flat and segmented) and trematodes (flukes, leaf-shaped). Eosinophilia is a common finding in tissue-invasive helminthiasis, whereas intestinal worms confined to the lumen usually do not cause it.

Nematodes. Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) causes perianal itching, and the scotch tape test detects eggs; it is transmitted fecal-orally and treated with albendazole or related drugs. Ascaris lumbricoides is the largest intestinal nematode; eggs are swallowed, larvae pass through lungs (cough, eosinophilia), and adults can obstruct the intestine or biliary tree. Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) causes rectal prolapse in heavy infection. Hookworms (Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale) enter through bare feet, pass through the lungs, and cause iron deficiency anemia by blood loss in the gut. Strongyloides stercoralis penetrates skin, and autoinfection allows persistence for decades; hyperinfection with Gram-negative sepsis occurs in people given corticosteroids, so patients from endemic areas should be treated before immunosuppression, with ivermectin. Toxocara canis causes visceral larva migrans with eosinophilia and hepatomegaly. Trichinella spiralis is acquired from undercooked pork (or wild game) and causes myalgia, periorbital edema and eosinophilia as larvae encyst in muscle. Filarial worms, transmitted by mosquitoes, include Wuchereria bancrofti (lymphatic filariasis, elephantiasis), Onchocerca volvulus (blackflies, river blindness and skin disease) and Loa loa (deer fly, migration of adult worms through the eye). Doxycycline targets the Wolbachia endosymbiont of
some filariae. Ancylostoma braziliense causes cutaneous larva migrans, a serpiginous itchy track on the foot.

Cestodes. Taenia saginata (beef) causes a mild intestinal infection. Taenia solium (pork) can cause intestinal tapeworm if cysts in meat are eaten, but if eggs from a carrier are swallowed, cysticerci form in tissue, and neurocysticercosis is a common cause of adult-onset seizures in endemic areas; imaging shows cystic lesions with a scolex. Diphyllobothrium latum from raw fish can cause vitamin B12 deficiency. Echinococcus granulosus, carried by dogs, causes hydatid cysts of the liver and lung; rupture can cause anaphylaxis, so cyst aspiration is performed with caution. Hymenolepis nana is a common dwarf tapeworm.

Trematodes. Schistosoma species are acquired by skin penetration of cercariae in freshwater with snail hosts. S. mansoni and S. japonicum infect mesenteric veins and cause hepatosplenic disease and portal hypertension; S. haematobium infects the vesical plexus and causes hematuria and an increased risk of squamous cell bladder carcinoma. Granulomas around eggs cause the pathology, and eggs have lateral spines (mansoni) or a terminal spine (haematobium). Clonorchis sinensis, from raw freshwater fish, predisposes to cholangiocarcinoma. Fasciola hepatica is acquired from watercress. Paragonimus westermani causes lung disease with hemoptysis resembling tuberculosis, from raw crabs. Praziquantel is the first-line drug for most trematodes and cestode infections (except for tissue stages of echinococcus), and albendazole and mebendazole block microtubule polymerisation in nematodes.

Worked example. A 28-year-old immigrant from Egypt has painless terminal hematuria. Urine microscopy shows eggs with a terminal spine. This is Schistosoma haematobium, and the long-term risk is squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

lessons.title: Sterilization, Infection Control, Antimicrobial Resistance and Diagnosis
body: Sterilization destroys all microbial life including spores. Autoclaving (steam under pressure, commonly 121 C for 15 to 30 minutes) is the standard method and is monitored with Geobacillus stearothermophilus spore indicators. Dry heat, ethylene oxide gas (for heat-sensitive devices), hydrogen peroxide plasma and radiation are other methods. Disinfection reduces organisms without necessarily killing spores: high-level disinfectants such as glutaraldehyde and ortho-phthalaldehyde are used for endoscopes, and intermediate or low-level agents (alcohol, chlorine, quaternary ammonium compounds) for surfaces. Antisepsis applies to skin: chlorhexidine and alcohol are common. Alcohol hand rubs are not sporicidal, so hand washing with soap and water is preferred for Clostridioides difficile and for norovirus outbreaks. Prions resist routine sterilisation and need special protocols.

Healthcare-associated infection control relies on hand hygiene and standard precautions for all patients, plus transmission-based precautions. Contact precautions apply to MRSA, vancomycin-resistant enterococci, C. difficile and resistant Gram-negatives. Droplet precautions apply to influenza, meningococcus and pertussis. Airborne precautions (negative-pressure room and respirator) apply to tuberculosis, measles and varicella. Device-related infections are prevented with bundles for central lines, urinary catheters and ventilators. Vaccination of health workers, postexposure prophylaxis (such as after needlestick injury from a hepatitis B, hepatitis C or HIV source), and surveillance are further tools. Antimicrobial stewardship aims to use the right agent for the right duration.

Resistance mechanisms fall into a few categories. Enzymatic inactivation: beta-lactamases (including ESBLs and carbapenemases), aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes and chloramphenicol acetyltransferase. Target alteration: mecA PBP2a in MRSA, vanA and vanB changing the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus to D-Ala-D-Lac in vancomycin-resistant enterococci, gyrase mutations for fluoroquinolones, ribosomal methylation for macrolides, and rpoB mutations for rifampin. Reduced permeability or increased efflux: porin loss in Pseudomonas, and tetracycline and multidrug efflux pumps. Bypass pathways, such as acquiring an insensitive dihydrofolate reductase. Resistance spreads by plasmids and transposons, and selection pressure from antibiotic use drives it; being resistant is not the same as being more virulent. Susceptibility testing reports minimum inhibitory concentration, the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth, and minimum bactericidal concentration is the lowest that kills.

The diagnostic laboratory uses staining (Gram, acid-fast, India ink, KOH), culture on selective, differential and enriched media, biochemical and mass spectrometry identification, antigen detection, serology (acute and convalescent titres with a fourfold rise indicating infection), and nucleic acid amplification tests. Specimen quality matters: sputum with many squamous epithelial cells is saliva, and blood culture needs adequate volume drawn before antibiotics, with multiple sets to separate a contaminant from true bacteremia. Test performance matters: sensitivity is the ability to detect true positives, specificity the ability to exclude true negatives, and predictive values depend on prevalence.

Worked example. An isolate of Enterococcus faecium grows despite vancomycin. The mechanism is replacement of the D-Ala-D-Ala target with D-Ala-D-Lac, which lowers vancomycin binding, so contact precautions are needed and alternative agents guided by susceptibility testing are used.

questions.prompt: Which structure accounts for the retention of crystal violet by Gram-positive bacteria after alcohol decolorisation?
choices: A thin peptidoglycan layer sandwiched beneath an outer membrane
A mycolic acid layer that resists decolorisation by acid and alcohol
A polysaccharide capsule that prevents penetration of the counterstain
A thick peptidoglycan layer that traps the crystal violet-iodine complex

questions.prompt: A drug is effective against Staphylococcus aureus but is too large to pass through porin channels. Which organism group will it most likely fail to treat?
choices: Spore-forming rods whose spores resist heat and desiccation
Gram-positive cocci with thick peptidoglycan and teichoic acids
Gram-negative rods with an outer membrane containing porins
Cell-wall-deficient organisms that lack peptidoglycan entirely

questions.prompt: Which statement about lipid A of lipopolysaccharide is correct?
choices: It is a heat-labile protein that inhibits elongation factor 2
It is the toxic component that activates TLR4 and drives septic shock
It is the teichoic acid that anchors the Gram-positive cell wall
It is the variable O antigen that determines serotype of each strain

questions.prompt: A 64-year-old woman has fever, hypotension and a urinary catheter. Blood cultures grow pink rods. Her low blood pressure is most directly caused by which bacterial component?
choices: Lipid A released from the outer membrane and sensed by macrophages
Peptidoglycan cross-links produced by transpeptidase enzymes in the wall
Teichoic acid that is shed and binds the Fc region of antibody
